opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a fundamental asymmetry, and it isn't unique to machine learning. It's true across security. The defender has to be right about everything, and the attacker only has to be right once. When you build a defense, you're implicitly claiming that no input, out of an astronomically large space, makes the model do the wrong thing. To break that claim, I just need to find one counterexample.

With neural networks the asymmetry is even worse, because we don't really understand what these models are doing internally. In traditional software security you can at least reason about the code. You can say this buffer has this length, so this check prevents an overflow. With a model that has billions of parameters, we have no clean specification of what "correct behavior" even means, let alone a proof that the model satisfies it. So most defenses end up being heuristics. They work against the attacks the designer thought of, and then someone comes along with an attack the designer didn't think of.

There's also a methodological issue I've spent a lot of time on. Historically, many defenses were evaluated against weak or non-adaptive attacks. Someone proposes a defense, tests it against the standard attack from a prior paper, and it holds up. But the right question isn't whether the old attack works. The right question is whether an attacker who knows exactly how your defense works can design something specifically to beat it. When you ask that question, a lot of defenses fall apart, sometimes within days. I've broken a fair number of published defenses, and usually it isn't because I'm especially clever. It's because the defense was never tested against someone actually trying.

And attacks are cheap to iterate on. If I'm attacking, I can try a thousand things, and failures cost me nothing. If you're defending, every change you make has costs. It might hurt accuracy, slow the system down, or make it less useful. So you're constrained in ways the attacker isn't.

None of this means defense is hopeless. But we should be honest that in adversarial machine learning, we mostly don't have defenses that provably work against motivated adversaries. So when you deploy these systems, you should design the surrounding system assuming the model can be fooled, rather than assuming the model itself will be robust.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts proving a defense across a huge input space with finding one counterexample, and notes that model behavior is poorly understood. It does not clearly state that establishing robustness requires a more accurate mental model of the system’s behavior than finding an attack.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the short version is that attacking is easy because the attacker only needs to find one thing that works, and the defender has to be right about everything.

When I'm attacking a system, I have this enormous freedom. I get to pick the inputs. I get to pick the strategy. If my first idea doesn't work, I try a second one, and a third, and a hundredth. I only have to succeed once. The defender, on the other hand, has to anticipate every one of those hundred ideas, including the ones nobody has thought of yet. That asymmetry is just structural. It's not specific to machine learning. It's true in cryptography, it's true in systems security, it's true everywhere. But it bites especially hard in machine learning.

And the reason it bites harder here is that we don't actually understand what these models are doing. In traditional security, when you find a buffer overflow, you can go fix the buffer overflow. You understand the bug, you understand the fix, and you can be fairly confident the specific bug is gone. With a neural network, when I find an adversarial example, there's no line of code to patch. The model is a few billion floating point numbers, and the vulnerability is some emergent property of how those numbers interact. So you end up with defenses that are, essentially, guesses. Someone has an intuition that if you add noise, or do some input transformation, or train in a particular way, the attacks will go away. And then I come along and I just... optimize against that intuition, and it falls over.

The thing I've found, over and over again, is that most published defenses weren't broken because the attack was clever. They were broken because the defense was evaluated against the attacks the defender already had in mind. If you build a defense and then test it with the exact same attack you were designing against, of course it looks good. But that's not what an adversary does. The adversary looks at your defense and designs a new attack specifically for it. So the evaluation has to be adaptive, and in practice very few are.

There's also a more fundamental point, which is that attacking is an optimization problem and we are extremely good at optimization. That's what the entire field is. Gradient descent is the hammer that built these models, and it's the same hammer that breaks them. I don't need some deep insight into why the model fails, I just need to write down a loss function that says "make the classifier wrong" and let the optimizer do the work. The defender doesn't have an equivalently powerful tool. There's no gradient descent for "make the model robust to things you haven't seen."

I do want to be careful not to make this sound hopeless, because I don't think it is. Adversarial training genuinely works, for a reasonable definition of works. It's just expensive, it costs you accuracy, and it only covers the threat model you trained for. And the thing I'd really like the field to internalize is that a defense claim is a claim about the absence of something. You're saying "no attack exists." That's a very strong statement, and the burden of evidence for it should be correspondingly high. Right now I think we're far too willing to accept "I tried a couple of things and they didn't work" as evidence of robustness. And as long as that's the standard, attacking is going to keep looking easy, because honestly, it is.

r001.rationale: The response says attackers can succeed through optimization without understanding why a model fails, while defenders must anticipate many attacks. It does not state that establishing robustness requires a more accurate mental model of the system’s behavior than finding one successful attack.

astra-6.text:
I think the fundamental asymmetry is that, as an attacker, I only need to find one thing that breaks the system. As a defender, you need to make sure that everything you’re trying to protect actually holds up against all the different things an attacker might try.

And the attacker gets to adapt. If you put a defense in place, I can look at what it does, try something, see why it fails, and change my approach. So a defense that stops the attacks you already know about isn’t necessarily a defense against someone who’s actively trying to get around it.

With AI systems, this is especially difficult because we don’t have a precise understanding of what they’ll do on every possible input. We train them to behave a certain way, and we can test that behavior, but that’s very different from having a guarantee. As an attacker, I get to look for the gap between the behavior you tested and the behavior the model actually has.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts finding one attack with defending against many, and notes that AI behavior is not precisely understood. It does not state that establishing robustness requires a more accurate mental model of the system than finding a working attack.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the fundamental asymmetry is that, as an attacker, I only have to find one thing that goes wrong. As a defender, you have to make sure that every possible thing someone might try is handled correctly. And the space of things you can ask a language model is enormous.

The other advantage is that I get to adapt. You build a defense, I try it, I see where it fails, and I change my attack. I can spend a lot of time finding one example that works, and then showing that example is very easy. Building a defense that generalizes beyond the attacks you already know about is much harder.

This isn’t unique to AI; we see it throughout computer security. But with AI, we also don’t have a very precise specification of what the system should do, or a clear separation between instructions and the untrusted data it’s processing. That makes it difficult even to state the property you want to defend, let alone guarantee it.

r001.rationale: The response says defenders must handle every possible attempt and that AI behavior lacks a precise specification, but it does not state that robustness requires a more accurate mental model of the system than finding one successful attack.
